{{short description|Graph which remains connected when k or fewer nodes removed}}
[[File:4-connected graph.svg|thumb|A graph with connectivity 4 and not 5: The graph remains connected whichever 3 vertices are removed but removing all but 2 opposing vertices (i.e. removing 4) leaves a disconnected graph.]]

In [[graph theory]], a connected [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] {{mvar|G}} is said to be '''{{mvar|k}}-vertex-connected''' (or '''{{mvar|k}}-connected''') if it has more than {{mvar|k}} [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] and remains [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] whenever fewer than {{mvar|k}} vertices are removed.

The '''vertex-connectivity''', or just '''connectivity''', of a graph is the largest {{mvar|k}} for which the graph is {{mvar|k}}-vertex-connected.

== Definitions ==
A graph (other than a [[complete graph]]) has connectivity ''k'' if ''k'' is the size of the smallest subset of vertices such that the graph becomes disconnected if you delete them.<ref name="Schrijver">{{Citation|author=Schrijver|title=Combinatorial Optimization|date=12 February 2003|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783540443896|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mqGeSQ6dJycC&q=%22k-vertex-connected+%22}}</ref> In [[complete graph]]s, there is no subset whose removal would disconnect the graph. Some sources modify the definition of connectivity to handle this case, by defining it as the size of the smallest subset of vertices whose deletion results in either a disconnected graph or a single vertex. For this variation, the connectivity of a complete graph <math>K_n</math> is <math>n-1</math>.<ref>{{citation|title=Line Graphs and Line Digraphs|volume=68|series=Developments in Mathematics|first1=Lowell W.|last1=Beineke|author-link=L. W. Beineke|first2=Jay S.|last2=Bagga|publisher=Springer Nature|year=2021|isbn=9783030813864|page=87|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=um1LEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA87}}</ref>

An equivalent definition is that a graph with at least two vertices is ''k''-connected if, for every pair of its vertices, it is possible to find ''k'' vertex-independent [[Path (graph theory)|paths]] connecting these vertices; see [[Menger's theorem]] {{Harv|Diestel|2005| p=55}}. This definition produces the same answer, ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1, for the connectivity of the complete graph ''K''<sub>''n''</sub>.<ref name="Schrijver"/>

A ''k''-connected graph is by definition [[Connected graph|connected]]; it is called [[Biconnected graph|biconnected]] for ''k'' ≥ 2 and triconnected for ''k'' ≥ 3.

== Applications ==

=== Components ===
Every graph decomposes into a disjoint union of [[Component (graph theory)|1-connected components]]. 1-connected graphs decompose into a tree of [[biconnected component]]s. 2-connected graphs decompose into a tree of [[triconnected component]]s.

=== Polyhedral combinatorics ===
The 1-[[Skeleton (topology)|skeleton]] of any ''k''-dimensional convex [[polytope]] forms a ''k''-vertex-connected graph ([[Balinski's theorem]]).<ref>{{citation
 | last = Balinski
 | first = M. L.
 | authorlink = Michel Balinski
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]]
 | pages = 431–434
 | title = On the graph structure of convex polyhedra in ''n''-space
 | volume = 11
 | year = 1961
 | doi = 10.2140/pjm.1961.11.431
 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> As a partial converse, [[Steinitz's theorem]] states that any 3-vertex-connected [[planar graph]] forms the skeleton of a convex [[polyhedron]].

== Computational complexity ==

The vertex-connectivity of an input graph ''G'' can be computed in polynomial time in the following way<ref>''The algorithm design manual'', p 506, and ''Computational discrete mathematics: combinatorics and graph theory with Mathematica'', p. 290-291</ref> consider all possible pairs <math>(s, t)</math> of nonadjacent nodes to disconnect, using [[Menger's theorem]] to justify that the minimal-size separator for <math>(s, t)</math> is the number of pairwise vertex-independent paths between them, encode the input by doubling each vertex as an edge to reduce to a computation of the number of pairwise edge-independent paths, and compute the maximum number of such paths by computing the [[maximum flow]] in the graph between <math>s</math> and <math>t</math> with capacity 1 to each edge, noting that a flow of <math>k</math> in this graph corresponds, by the [[integral flow theorem]], to <math>k</math> pairwise edge-independent paths from <math>s</math> to <math>t</math>.

==Properties==
Let {{mvar|k≥2}}.
* Every <math>k</math>-connected graph of order at least <math>2k</math> contains a [[cycle (graph theory)|cycle]] of length at least <math>2k</math>
* In a <math>k</math>-connected graph, any <math>k</math> vertices in <math>G</math> lie on a common [[cycle (graph theory)|cycle]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Diestel|2016}}, p.84</ref>

The [[cycle space]] of a <math>3</math>-connected graph is generated by its non-separating [[induced path|induced cycles]].
<ref>{{harvtxt|Diestel|2012}}, p.65.</ref>

==''k''-linked graph ==
A graph with at least <math>2k</math> vertices is called '''<math>k</math>-linked''' if there are <math>k</math> disjoint paths for any sequences
<math>a_1,\dots,a_k</math> and <math>b_1,\dots, b_k</math> of <math>2k</math> distinct vertices. Every <math>k</math>-linked graph is <math>(2k-1)</math>-connected graph, but not necessarily <math>2k</math>-connected. <ref>{{harvtxt|Diestel|2016}}, p.85</ref>

If a graph is <math>2k</math>-connected and has average degree of at least <math>16k</math>, then it is <math>k</math>-linked.
<ref>{{harvtxt|Diestel|2016}}, p.75</ref>
